sections.title: A settlement raised by centuries
sections.body: Erbil Citadel stands on an oval mound above the surrounding city in Iraq's Kurdistan region. The mound, known as a tell, formed as successive generations built and rebuilt in roughly the same place. Its height records a long history of settlement rather than a single construction project. The citadel's walls and rooftops still give a strong impression of an enclosed town overlooking newer streets.

sections.title: Ancient Arbela and later Erbil
sections.body: Erbil is associated with ancient Arbela, an important Assyrian centre. Archaeological evidence and historical accounts point to occupation across many periods, although the visible buildings cannot all be dated to those earliest communities. Later street arrangements and houses reflect changing ways of living. Distinguishing buried layers from surviving façades helps avoid presenting the citadel as one unchanged ancient fortress.

sections.title: Streets behind the walls
sections.body: A line of tall nineteenth-century façades helps create the citadel's defensive appearance. Within it, streets have a distinctive fan-like arrangement associated with the late Ottoman period. These features reveal how homes, access routes and public spaces fitted together on a confined hilltop. Their value lies in the pattern of the settlement as well as in the architecture of individual buildings.

sections.title: Repairing a living urban landmark
sections.body: Historic fabric can be damaged by neglected drainage, structural movement and inappropriate replacement materials. Conservation needs archaeological records and careful decisions about future use, rather than making the site look artificially new. Erbil Citadel offers a way to read several periods of urban history in one place, while remembering that the surrounding modern city is part of its continuing story.

sections.title: Islands with an unusual natural history
sections.body: The Socotra Archipelago lies in the north-western Indian Ocean near the Gulf of Aden. Its islands and rocky islets are separated from many neighbouring habitats by open water. That isolation, together with varied landscapes, has allowed an extraordinary number of plants and animals to evolve locally. Socotra is therefore much more than a dramatic landscape of unusual trees.

sections.title: Species found nowhere else
sections.body: Many of Socotra's plant species are endemic, as are exceptionally high proportions of its reptiles and land snails. Such species may depend on particular soils, slopes or moisture conditions. Their restricted ranges make them scientifically valuable but also vulnerable to rapid environmental change. Studying the archipelago helps explain how geography and long periods of separation shape biodiversity.

sections.title: Connections with the sea
sections.body: The surrounding waters contain coral communities, fish and other marine life. Seabirds and migrating birds also use the islands, linking them to routes across the wider region. Coastal ecosystems face different pressures from those of the inland plateaux and mountains. Protecting the archipelago requires understanding these connections rather than concentrating only on its most photographed plants.

sections.title: Conservation with communities
sections.body: The islands have human communities and local knowledge, so conservation cannot treat them as an empty scientific reserve. Changes in land use, introduced species and pressures on marine habitats can affect the ecological balance. Monitoring remote places is difficult, and protecting them requires long-term attention. Socotra shows how biological distinctiveness depends on both geography and the choices made about land and sea.

records.hook: Saint Kitts and Nevis — Brimstone Hill Fortress National Park

sections.title: A fortress above the Caribbean
sections.body: Brimstone Hill rises steeply above the coast of Saint Kitts, where a large fortress occupies a commanding position. Its height allowed artillery to cover approaches and made the site important in European struggles for control of Caribbean islands. The walls are not simply a scenic lookout: they belong to a history of military competition, plantation economies and colonial expansion.

sections.title: Built through unequal power
sections.body: British military engineers planned much of the fortification, while enslaved Africans carried out the labour that made its construction possible. The stonework therefore records technical skill alongside exploitation. Recognising who worked on the site changes how its imposing appearance should be understood. The fortress was part of a colonial society whose wealth and military priorities depended heavily on coerced labour.

sections.title: Engineering on a volcanic hill
sections.body: The complex includes bastions, gun positions and buildings arranged across different levels of the slope. Local stone helped form substantial walls, while the steep terrain created both defensive advantages and practical construction difficulties. Routes between the structures show how soldiers and supplies moved through the site. Its design responded to the landscape instead of imposing a regular plan on flat ground.

sections.title: A place for careful interpretation
sections.body: Brimstone Hill has to be maintained against tropical weather, vegetation and wear from visitors. Conservation should protect original material while explaining the lives of enslaved builders and the communities affected by colonial conflict. The park is an opportunity to discuss Caribbean history through its landscape and surviving structures, rather than treating the fortress as a monument to military success alone.

sections.title: Two peaks beside the sea
sections.body: Gros Piton and Petit Piton rise sharply above the south-western coast of Saint Lucia near Soufrière. Their shapes are remnants of volcanic activity, and they dominate a landscape of ridges, steep slopes and sheltered bays. The World Heritage property includes more than the two peaks: nearby forests, geothermal features and coastal waters help explain the area's unusual physical geography.

sections.title: Evidence of volcanic forces
sections.body: Hot springs and sulphurous fumaroles show that the region's geological story is not confined to distant eruptions. The Pitons belong to a larger volcanic complex formed by processes beneath the Lesser Antilles. Their contrasting rock forms offer visible clues to the history of that system. Geological features need protection because careless development can alter the setting in which they are understood.

sections.title: Forests meeting reefs
sections.body: Vegetation changes with height, from tropical forest on lower slopes to specialised communities near exposed summits. Offshore, coral reefs support fish and other marine species. Runoff from land can affect these underwater habitats, so conservation must connect forest management with the condition of the sea. The area illustrates how a small coastal region can contain several closely linked ecosystems.

sections.title: People and protection
sections.body: The Pitons are an important part of Saint Lucian identity and a major attraction for visitors. The protected area also includes land used by residents, so planning must consider housing, livelihoods and access alongside conservation. Tourism and building pressure can threaten views and habitats if poorly managed. The strongest protection treats the landscape as a shared place rather than a photograph of two mountains.
